title: Chapter 154: Dog Cage?
html:
“Psychiatric hospitals provide a different kind of care from ordinary hospitals, and they carry a far heavier stigma. Most people instinctively keep their distance,” Chen Ge told the camera. “That much is undeniable. The patients treated here may differ from us, but sometimes it is difficult to say whether they are abnormal—or whether we are simply no more normal than they are.”

The moment his feet touched the ground, his expression grew focused. “The hospital behind me is the source of countless horrifying rumors. After nightfall, strange screams echo from its empty buildings. Messages written in blood appear along corridors where no living person walks. The director vanished without a trace, and some believe he still hides in one of the hospital’s darkest corners.”

He glanced at the chat. Most viewers were unconvinced, and several openly compared his stream to Qin Guang’s.

“Supernatural livestream, yet another actor trying to lie to us.”

“I can see your future even through the screen. Some hosts tell ghost stories only so we’ll remember them after they’re gone.”

“I follow the story, but why are you holding a rooster? Are you combining a supernatural stream with a cooking show? Is this some new genre?”

“Visiting a mental hospital at night? Based on that, you got my like!”

The viewers joked among themselves, displaying a conspicuous lack of fear.

“A live rooster can ward off negative energy. Tonight, I’ll show you what genuine fear feels like. It took us two hours just to find this hospital. Doesn’t that frighten any of you?” Chen Ge explained patiently, but the audience remained skeptical.

“What is there to be afraid of? The last host who said that is now fixing his car.”

“Wow! That is such a cute cat…”

Their banter helped settle his nerves. After chatting a little longer, he began exploring the Jiujiang Third Psychological Convalescence Centre. A concrete wall enclosed the vast grounds. The large courtyard had probably once given patients room to exercise, but years of neglect had left everything except a few concrete paths buried beneath knee-high weeds.

Farther in, he finally saw the three interconnected buildings, arranged in the shape of the Chinese character 品. The middle building projected northward, and covered corridors linked all three.

“The first two sick halls face the sun, so the building turned away from it must be the Third Sick Hall. What a strange design. Were some of those patients forbidden from seeing daylight?”

The layout alone made his skin crawl. There must be a reason they designed it this way. Whether for the Trial Mission or my parents’ clues, I have to enter the Third Sick Hall tonight.

The white cat followed as he advanced. A full moon washed the concrete in milky light. At the top of the steps to the first sick hall stood a steel entrance door. One push sent it swinging open.

“The lock is broken.” His previous Trial Missions had taught him what to examine. Shining his flashlight on the mechanism, he said, “The spring snapped. Someone forced their way inside.”

He stared down the dark corridor as a question surfaced. “Who broke in?”

Someone had returned after the hospital closed. Was it one of the former patients—or his parents?

Director Luo had heard his parents mention the Third Sick Hall before their disappearance, and the bloody note left in the park pointed to the same place. Yet Chen Ge still did not understand what made it special.

His parents had discussed the hospital before vanishing, while the bloody note appeared only afterward. What happened to them inside the Third Sick Hall?

He pushed the steel door fully open. Rubbish and abandoned beds cluttered the corridor, offering a glimpse of the institution’s past. When it operated, overcrowding had apparently forced many patients to sleep in the hallways.

Unlike a general hospital, this facility contained few clearly designated rooms. Unmarked doors lined the crowded corridor. Chen Ge sniffed and caught a familiar stench—the same odor he had detected at Hai Ming Apartments, clinging to Wang Shenglong.

“I haven’t even entered properly, and the oppressive energy is already this strong.” It was his first time inside a psychiatric hospital, and the patient’s crude map was his only guide.

“The three halls should share a basic layout, and this first building ought to be the safest. I’ll learn the terrain here before moving deeper.” He had taken only one step when the white cat leaped onto his shoulder, seemingly desperate to communicate something he could not understand.

“This is the first time you’ve willingly come this close to me. What did you sense? Are you frightened, or is it something else?”

Something crunched beneath every step. Looking down, he saw the shells of countless unidentified insects packed between the cracked tiles. The hospital had stood abandoned for years, so pesticide could not explain their deaths. What had killed them?

Every door in the first sick hall stood open, revealing nearly identical rooms: cramped spaces containing nothing but narrow beds.

“How many patients did they keep here?” Chen Ge entered one room to inspect it. Four wooden beds filled the tiny space, leaving barely enough room for him to turn around.

“Living in a box like this day after day could drive anyone mad.” He left and soon reached the first junction, where a wooden counter marked what appeared to be a nurses’ station. Empty medicine bottles and cards bearing patients’ names littered its surface.

“The patients must have collected their daily medication here.” Looking behind the counter, he found two objects that did not belong.

Two cages made of welded iron bars stood inside. Each was barely large enough for a medium-sized dog.

“What were these cages used for?” Chen Ge climbed over the counter. When his flashlight swept across the bars, he discovered something startling: a half-cooked, partially plucked duck lay inside one cage.

“There’s no decay. Someone put this here recently.” Gripping his mallet, Chen Ge pressed his back to the wall. “I’m not alone in this hospital.”
